sources.excerpt: # [![Github Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/tag/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts.svg?filter=v*&sort=semver&label=github)](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/releases/latest) [![NPM Package](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@openzeppelin/contracts.svg)](https://www.npmjs.org/package/@openzeppelin/contracts) [![Coverage Status](https://codecov.io/gh/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts) [![GitPOAPs](https://public-api.gitpoap.io/v1/repo/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/badge)](https://www.gitpoap.io/gh/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-%F0%9F%93%84-yellow)](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts) [![Forum](https://img.shields.io/badge/forum-%F0%9F%92%AC-yellow)](https://forum.openzeppelin.com/) **A library for secure smart contract development.** Build on a solid foundation of community-vetted code. * Implementations of standards like [ERC20](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/erc20) and [ERC721](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/erc721). * Flexible [role-based permissioning](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/access-control) scheme. * Reusable [Solidity components](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/utilities) to build custom contracts and complex decentralized systems. :mage: **Not sure how to get started?** Check out [Contracts Wizard](https://wizard.openzeppelin.com/) — an interactive smart contract generator. :building_construction: **Want to scale your decentralized application?** Check out [OpenZeppelin Defender](https://openzeppelin.com/defender) — a mission-critical developer security platform to code, audit, deploy, monitor, and operate with confidence. > [!IMPORTANT] > OpenZeppelin Contracts uses semantic versioning to communicate backwards compatibility of its API and storage layout. For upgradeable contracts, the storage layout of different major versions should be assumed incompatible, for example, it is unsafe to upgrade from 4.9.3 to 5.0.0. Learn more at [Backwards Compatibility](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/backwards-compatibility). ## Overview ### Installation #### Hardhat (npm) ``` $ npm install @openzeppelin/contracts ``` #### Foundry (git) > [!WARNING] > When installing via git, it is a common error to use the `master` branch. This is a development branch that should be avoided in favor of tagged releases. The release process involves security measures that the `master` branch does not guarantee. > [!WARNING] > Foundry installs the latest version initially, but subsequent `forge update` commands will use the `master` branch. ``` $ forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts ``` Add `@openzeppelin/contracts/=lib/openzeppelin-contracts/contracts/` in `remappings.txt.` ### Usage Once installed, you can use the contracts in the library by importing them: ```solidity pragma solidity ^0.8.20; import {ERC721} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol"; contract MyCollectible is ERC721 { constructor() ERC721("MyCollectible", "MCO") { } } ``` _If you're new to smart contract development, head to [Developing Smart Contracts](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/learn/developing-smart-contracts) to learn about creating a new project and compiling your contracts._ To keep your system secure, you should **always** use the installed code as-is, and neither copy-paste it from online sources nor modify it yourself. The library is designed so that only the contracts and functions you use are deployed, so you don't need to worry about it needlessly increasing gas costs. ## Learn More The guides in the [documentation site](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts) will teach about different concepts, and how to use the related contracts that OpenZeppelin Contracts provides: * [Access Control](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/access-control): decide who can perform each of the actions on your system. * [Tokens](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/tokens): create tradeable assets or collectives, and distribute them via [Crowdsales](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/crowdsales). * [Utilities](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/utilities): generic useful tools including non-overflowing math, signature verification, and trustless paying systems. The [full API](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/api/token/ERC20) is also thoroughly documented, and serves as a great reference when developing your smart contract application. You can also ask for help or follow Contracts' development in the [community forum](https://forum.openzeppelin.com). Finally, you may want to take a look at the [guides on our blog](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/), which cover several common use cases and good practices. analysis.summary: Ownable is an abstract access-control module that designates a single owner and exposes an onlyOwner modifier for restricting functions. The owner can transfer ownership or renounce it; renouncing sets the owner to address(0), which the source states disables any owner-only functionality.

claims.statement: Ownable provides an onlyOwner modifier that inheriting contracts can apply to restrict function access to the owner account.
claims.quote:
It will make available the modifier
 * `onlyOwner`, which can be applied to your functions to restrict their use to
the owner.

claims.statement: renounceOwnership can only be called by the current owner and sets the owner to address(0).
After renunciation, owner-only functions can no longer be called, so any functionality gated by onlyOwner becomes permanently unavailable.
claims.quote:
NOTE: Renouncing ownership will leave the contract without an owner,
     * thereby disabling any functionality that is only available to the owner.

limitations: The excerpt covers only the Ownable module itself; it does not enumerate which specific functions in inheriting contracts are owner-gated.
The source does not describe recovery mechanisms after renunciation, so the permanence of the effect is inferred from the absence of an owner rather than stated as a recovery guarantee.

checks.scope: Schema and exact quotation checks only. Quotation presence does not establish semantic entailment.

analysis.summary: Pausable is an abstract module that stores a paused flag, exposes paused(), provides whenNotPaused/whenPaused modifiers and internal _pause/_unpause functions with events and custom errors. It does not automatically gate any function; callers must apply modifiers and wire up authorization and pause triggers themselves.

claims.statement: Pausable provides the whenNotPaused and whenPaused modifiers, the paused() view, and internal _pause/_unpause functions that set the flag and emit Paused/Unpaused events.
claims.quote:
It will make available the
 * modifiers `whenNotPaused` and `whenPaused`, which can be applied to
 * the functions of your contract.

claims.statement: Including the module alone does not make any function pausable; the caller must apply the modifiers to the functions it wants gated.
claims.quote:
Note that they will not be pausable by
 * simply including this module, only once the modifiers are put in place.

claims.statement: Because _pause and _unpause are internal and the module only checks the paused flag, the caller is responsible for access control over who can trigger pausing and for choosing which functions to guard.

limitations: The excerpt does not show any access-control mechanism (e.g., onlyOwner) on _pause/_unpause, so authorization requirements are inferred from their internal visibility rather than stated explicitly.
No security guarantee is implied; the excerpt is a single revision of one file and does not cover inheriting contracts or deployment configuration.

analysis.summary: The supplied files are OpenZeppelin library modules (Ownable, Pausable) and a README. They establish the intended mechanics of these reusable components and some library-level guidance, but they do not demonstrate that any deployed or integrating application is secure.

claims.statement: Ownable restricts functions using an onlyOwner modifier that reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount when the caller is not the owner.
Pausable's pause/unpause modifiers only take effect if an integrating contract applies them to its functions.
claims.quote:
Note that they will not be pausable by
 * simply including this module, only once the modifiers are put in place.

claims.statement: The README advises using installed library code as-is rather than copying or modifying it, which is guidance about library usage, not evidence that a specific integration is secure.
claims.quote: To keep your system secure, you should **always** use the installed code as-is, and neither copy-paste it from online sources nor modify it yourself.

limitations: No integrating application code is provided, so access-control wiring, owner key management, pause coverage, and upgrade/storage-layout compatibility cannot be assessed.
The README excerpt is truncated, so its full guidance is not available.
These sources cannot establish absence of vulnerabilities or overall security of any deployment.

review.summary: All three draft entries are grounded in the supplied excerpts and correctly scoped. Observations match the source text: Ownable's onlyOwner/_checkOwner revert behavior, renounceOwnership setting owner to address(0), Pausable's modifiers/internal _pause/_unpause and the explicit note that inclusion alone does not make functions pausable. Inferences are labeled and reasonable (permanence after renunciation, caller responsibility for access control over internal pause hooks). The evidence-live entry properly frames README guidance as usage advice rather than proof of integration security, and limitations correctly note the truncated README, absent integrating application, and inability to establish absence of vulnerabilities. No unsupported security assurances, contradictions, or out-of-scope claims found.
